Implement the trie from scratch for the first one without looking at the lesson code, then draw the trie for the words cat, car, card and dog on paper and mark the end-of-word flags.
checks: Why does search need the end-of-word flag if the path exists?
A path can exist as a prefix of longer words without being a word itself. The flag distinguishes a stored word from a mere prefix.
What is the time complexity of trie search, and what does it depend on?
O(L) where L is the length of the word — it depends only on the word, not on how many words the trie contains.
How does autocomplete work on a trie?
Walk to the node for the typed prefix, then depth-first collect every complete word in that subtree, using the end-of-word flags.
When is a hash set better than a trie?
For exact membership only: it uses less memory and hashes the whole string in one step. A trie earns its cost when prefixes, ordering or prefix counts matter.
interview: Design autocomplete for a search box. What structure and why?
A trie: insert all terms, then for each typed prefix walk to its node and collect the words in its subtree. Lookup cost depends on prefix length, not dictionary size.
How does a trie make Word Search II tractable?
Build a trie of all dictionary words, then DFS the board following trie edges — any path that is not a prefix of some word is pruned immediately instead of explored.
cards: Trie
A tree storing strings as character paths, where words sharing a prefix share nodes — built for prefix queries.
Trie node
A node holding a map from character to child node plus an end-of-word flag.
End-of-word flag
Marks that a complete stored word ends at this node, distinguishing words from mere prefixes.
Prefix query
Checking whether any stored word starts with a given string — a single walk down the trie.
Autocomplete
Walking to a prefix node and collecting all complete words in its subtree.
Trie vs hash set
Hash sets win exact lookup on memory; tries win anything involving prefixes, ordering or prefix counts.

lessons.t: CSS Grid & Flexbox Deep — Layout Like a Professional
lessons.sub: Two layout systems, one decision
lessons.goal: By the end you can build two-dimensional layouts with grid-template-areas and fr units, make grids responsive with auto-fit and minmax, align precisely with Flexbox, and choose between Grid and Flexbox with reasons.
lessons.body:
1. Grid areas: draw the layout in text

grid-template-areas lets you sketch a layout as ASCII art: each quoted string is a row, each name is a region, and repeating a name spans it across cells. Assign children with grid-area and the page skeleton — header, sidebar, main, footer — is readable at a glance. Rearranging for mobile becomes rewriting the sketch inside a media query instead of touching the HTML. It is the most maintainable way to build app shells and dashboards, where the layout itself is the design.

2. fr units, auto-fit and minmax: grids that size themselves

The fr unit divides leftover space proportionally: 1fr 2fr gives the second column twice the first, after fixed sizes and gaps are subtracted. Combined with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)), a grid fits as many columns of at least 240px as the container allows and stretches them to fill — a fully responsive card grid with zero media queries. Skillzify's lesson cards use exactly this thinking: equal-height rows where every card in a row matches, whatever the screen width.

3. Flexbox alignment, properly understood

Flexbox confusion almost always comes from forgetting that the axes swap with flex-direction. In a row, justify-content works horizontally and align-items vertically; in a column they trade places. flex-grow distributes leftover space to items that ask for it, flex-shrink decides who gives space back, and flex-basis sets the starting size. The professional habit: use gap for spacing instead of margins on children, and let margin-left: auto push one item to the far end of a nav bar — the two tricks that replace most alignment hacks.

4. Grid or Flexbox: the decision rule

Grid is for layout in two dimensions where rows and columns must align with each other: page skeletons, card grids, dashboards. Flexbox is for one dimension where items flow and wrap: nav bars, button rows, chip lists, centring a single element. The test is whether the items need to line up across rows. If a card in row two must align with the card above it, that is Grid; if items can be different widths and simply flow, that is Flexbox. Real pages use both — Grid for the page, Flexbox inside each region — and knowing which layer you are in is most of professional layout.

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "nav nav"
    "side main"
    "side foot";
  gap: 16px;
}
.nav { grid-area: nav; }
.side { grid-area: side; }
.main { grid-area: main; }
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));
  gap: 14px;
}
lessons.task: Rebuild a page layout twice: first with grid-template-areas for a nav, sidebar, main and footer skeleton that rearranges to a single column under 700px by rewriting only the areas. Then build a card grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) and resize the browser to watch columns appear and disappear with no media queries at all.
checks: What does 1fr 2fr mean in grid-template-columns?
After fixed sizes and gaps are subtracted, the leftover space is split into three parts: the first column gets one part, the second gets two.
How does repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) make a grid responsive without media queries?
The browser fits as many columns of at least 240px as the container allows and stretches them equally to fill the row, adding or removing columns as the width changes.
Why do justify-content and align-items seem to swap in a column flex container?
They are defined relative to the main and cross axes, and flex-direction: column makes the main axis vertical — so justify works vertically and align horizontally.
When must a layout be Grid rather than Flexbox?
When items must align across both rows and columns — page skeletons and card grids. Flexbox flows items in one dimension without cross-row alignment.
interview: Explain the difference between Grid and Flexbox in one minute.

Grid lays out in two dimensions with rows and columns that align; Flexbox lays out in one dimension along a single axis. Use Grid for page structure and card grids, Flexbox for nav bars, rows and centring.
How do you make equal-height cards in a row?
With Grid's default stretch alignment and grid-auto-rows: 1fr, every card fills its row height; inside the card, a flex column with the footer pushed down by margin-top: auto keeps actions aligned.
cards: grid-template-areas
A way to define a grid layout as named text rows, so the page skeleton reads like a sketch and rearranges by rewriting the sketch.
fr unit
A fraction of the leftover space in a grid container, after fixed tracks and gaps are subtracted.
auto-fit + minmax
A responsive grid recipe: fit as many columns of at least a minimum size as possible, stretching them to fill.
Main axis
The direction Flexbox lays items out — horizontal for row, vertical for column; justify-content works along it.
flex-grow / shrink / basis
How a flex item claims leftover space, gives space back under pressure, and its starting size before either happens.
Grid vs Flexbox rule
Two dimensions with cross-row alignment: Grid. One dimension with flowing items: Flexbox.

lessons.t: DOM Deep — Building & Updating UI Without a Framework
lessons.sub: The manual rendering React automates
lessons.goal: By the end you can build elements with createElement and templates, attach one delegated listener for a whole list, re-render efficiently without wiping state, and carry data on elements with dataset.
lessons.body:
1. Building elements: createElement versus innerHTML

There are two ways to put markup on a page. innerHTML parses a string of HTML — fast to write, but dangerous with untrusted data because injected markup runs as real HTML, which is the classic cross-site scripting hole. createElement builds nodes one by one and sets text with textContent, which can never be interpreted as markup. The professional rule: use template strings with innerHTML only for markup you fully control, and textContent for anything a user typed. Skillzify renders lesson titles and user content through safe paths for exactly this reason.

2. Templates and fragments: build once, insert once

Appending elements to the live DOM one at a time forces the browser to recalculate layout repeatedly. A DocumentFragment is an off-screen container: build the whole list inside it, then append the fragment once, and the browser does a single layout pass. The template element goes further — its content is inert markup you clone per item with cloneNode(true), fill in, and append. Together they are how vanilla code renders a 250-lesson list smoothly without a framework.

3. Event delegation: one listener, whole list

Attaching a click handler to every card in a list wastes memory and breaks the moment items are re-rendered. Delegation attaches one listener to the parent instead: clicks bubble up, and event.target.closest("[data-lesson-id]") finds which card was clicked. Items added later work automatically, because the listener lives on the parent that never changes. This is the pattern Skillzify's pages use for lesson lists, exercise cards and reference entries — one listener per list, whatever its size.

4. Re-rendering without destroying state

The naive re-render — wipe the container and rebuild everything — loses scroll position, focus, and any text typed into inputs. Efficient vanilla rendering updates surgically: change only the text or class that changed, reuse existing nodes keyed by id, and rebuild only the section whose data actually changed. dataset supports this by carrying ids and state on the elements themselves, readable in handlers without a parallel lookup table. Mastering this is understanding, by hand, the exact problem React's virtual DOM automates — which is why it makes framework behaviour predictable later.

const list = document.querySelector("#lessons");
const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();

for (const lesson of lessons) {
  const card = document.createElement("article");
  card.className = "card";
  card.dataset.lessonId = lesson.id;
  const title = document.createElement("h3");
  title.textContent = lesson.title;
  card.appendChild(title);
  frag.appendChild(card);
}
list.appendChild(frag);

list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const card = e.target.closest("[data-lesson-id]");
  if (card) openLesson(card.dataset.lessonId);
});
lessons.task: Build a lesson list page in vanilla JavaScript: render 20 lesson cards from an array using a DocumentFragment and textContent, handle clicks with one delegated listener on the parent that reads data-lesson-id, and add a button that updates only the XP text of one card without re-rendering the list. Verify in DevTools that only one listener exists on the parent.
checks: Why is textContent safer than innerHTML for user data?
textContent inserts the value as pure text that is never parsed as markup, so injected tags cannot execute. innerHTML parses the string as HTML, which is the XSS hole.
What does a DocumentFragment buy you?
You build many nodes off-screen and insert them in one append, so the browser runs one layout pass instead of one per element.
Why does delegation keep working for items added later?
The listener is on the parent, and clicks bubble up from any child — including children created after the listener was attached.
What does a full wipe-and-rebuild re-render destroy?
Scroll position, focus, text typed into inputs, and any transient element state — which is why surgical updates are preferred.
interview: Explain event delegation and when you would use it.
Attach one listener to a parent and use event bubbling plus closest() to identify the clicked child. Use it for lists and grids: fewer listeners, and dynamically added items work without rebinding.
How do you render a large list efficiently without a framework?
Build nodes in a DocumentFragment with createElement and textContent, insert once, delegate events on the parent, and update surgically by id instead of rebuilding everything.

Building a DOM node programmatically, with textContent for safe text — the XSS-proof way to render user data.
DocumentFragment
An off-screen container for building many nodes before a single insertion, avoiding repeated layout work.
template element
Inert markup in the page that you clone per item, fill in, and append — a reusable node blueprint.
Event delegation
One listener on a parent handling events from all children via bubbling and closest().
dataset
The data-* attributes on an element, readable and writable in JavaScript — a place to carry ids and state on the node itself.
Surgical update
Changing only the nodes whose data changed, preserving scroll, focus and input state instead of rebuilding the whole list.

lessons.t: Python OOP Deep — Dunder Methods, Dataclasses & Protocols
lessons.sub: Classes that behave like built-ins
lessons.goal: By the end you can implement dunder methods like __repr__, __eq__ and __len__, replace boilerplate classes with @dataclass, type duck-typed interfaces with typing.Protocol, and expose controlled attributes with properties.
lessons.body:
1. Dunder methods: the protocol behind the syntax

Python's operators are method calls in disguise. len(obj) calls __len__, obj == other calls __eq__, printing calls __repr__ or __str__, and for x in obj calls __iter__. Implementing these double-underscore methods makes your classes behave like built-in types everywhere — in f-strings, in sets, in sorted(). Two rules matter most: __repr__ should be an unambiguous developer representation (ideally valid Python that recreates the object), and defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes instances unhashable, which surprises everyone exactly once.

2. Dataclasses: kill the boilerplate

Most classes exist to hold data, and hand-writing __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for each is pure boilerplate. The @dataclass decorator generates all three from annotated fields, with options like frozen=True for immutability (which also restores hashability) and field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults — never use a bare list as a default, or every instance shares it. A dataclass is still a normal class: add methods freely, and reach for __post_init__ when fields need validation or derivation at construction.

3. Protocols: duck typing, checked

Python has always allowed duck typing: if it has the right methods, it fits, whatever its class. typing.Protocol makes that contract explicit and checkable: declare a protocol with the methods you need, and any class with those methods satisfies it — no inheritance required. A type checker then verifies callers only pass objects with the right shape. This is structural typing, and it is how you write flexible code (anything drawable, anything with a read method) without a tangle of abstract base classes.

4. Properties: attributes with a gatekeeper

A property looks like a plain attribute from outside but runs code on access: the getter computes or validates, the setter rejects bad values. The pattern is a private _xp field behind a public xp property that refuses negatives. Properties let you start with a plain attribute and add validation later without changing any calling code — the Pythonic answer to the getter/setter ceremony other languages force from day one. Use them when an invariant must hold; do not wrap every attribute by reflex.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Lesson:
    id: str
    title: str
    xp: int = 20
    tags: tuple = ()

class Progress:
    def __init__(self):
        self._xp = 0

    @property
    def xp(self):
        return self._xp

    @xp.setter
    def xp(self, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("xp cannot be negative")
        self._xp = value

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Progress(xp={self._xp})"
lessons.task: Write a Lesson dataclass with frozen=True and confirm two equal lessons compare equal and can live in a set. Then write a Progress class with an xp property that rejects negatives and a __repr__, and try assigning a negative value to see the error. Finish by defining a small Protocol for anything with a render method and passing two unrelated classes through it.
checks: What happens when you define __eq__ but not __hash__?
Instances become unhashable, so they cannot be used in sets or as dict keys. Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None unless you also define it (or use a frozen dataclass).
Why must mutable dataclass defaults use default_factory?
A bare list default would be shared by every instance, so appending to one object's list would change them all. default_factory creates a fresh value per instance.
How does a Protocol differ from an abstract base class?
A protocol is structural: any class with the right methods satisfies it without inheriting anything. An ABC requires explicit subclassing. Protocols formalise duck typing.
When is a property worth adding over a plain attribute?
When an invariant must hold — validation, clamping, or a computed value — or when you need to add that logic later without changing callers.
interview: Explain __repr__ versus __str__.

__repr__ is the unambiguous developer representation, ideally recreating the object; __str__ is the friendly user-facing text. If only one is defined, define __repr__ — Python falls back to it for str.
Why choose a dataclass over a hand-written class?
It generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from the field declarations, removing boilerplate and its bugs, with options for immutability and ordering when needed.
cards: Dunder method
A double-underscore method like __len__ or __eq__ that Python calls for operators and built-ins, letting classes behave like built-in types.
__repr__
The unambiguous developer representation of an object, ideally valid Python that recreates it.
Dataclass
A class decorated with @dataclass that generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated fields.
frozen dataclass
An immutable dataclass whose instances are hashable and cannot be modified after creation.
Protocol
A structural interface from typing: any class with the declared methods satisfies it, with no inheritance required.
Property
An attribute that runs getter and setter code on access, enforcing invariants behind plain attribute syntax.

lessons.t: Node Testing Deep — node:test, Supertest & Coverage
lessons.sub: Test the API without a browser
lessons.goal: By the end you can write tests with the built-in node:test runner, exercise Express routes with Supertest, mock external calls, and generate and read a coverage report.
lessons.body:
1. node:test: the runner you already have

Since Node 18, a test runner ships with Node itself: node --test discovers files matching the test patterns, runs them, and reports pass or fail with no dependencies to install. Tests are plain functions using test() and describe() from node:test, with assertions from node:assert/strict. For a small service this is often all you need — no framework weight, no version churn — and it runs identically in CI because it is part of the runtime you already deploy.

2. Supertest: HTTP calls without a network

Testing an Express route by starting a real server and curling it is slow and flaky. Supertest instead hands your app object a fake HTTP layer: you write request(app).post("/api/tutor").send({...}) and assert on the status and JSON body, all in-process. The app never binds a port, tests run in parallel safely, and a failure shows the exact response. The one structural requirement: export the app separately from the code that listens, so tests can import the app without starting a server — a refactor Skillzify's server would need before its first route test.

3. Mocking the outside world

A route that calls Gemini must not call the real Gemini in tests: it is slow, costs quota, and returns different text every time. Mock at the boundary — replace the API client with a stub that returns a fixed reply, and assert your route handles success, empty input and upstream failure. node:test includes mock.fn() for this. The discipline from unit testing applies unchanged: mock external services, never the code under test, and keep one clearly-labelled live smoke test separate if you need end-to-end confidence.

4. Coverage: finding the untested branches

Node's built-in coverage (node --experimental-test-coverage, or c8 for richer reports) shows which lines and branches your tests executed. Read it as a map of blind spots: the error branch of the rate limiter, the 400 path of a validator — the code most likely to break in production and least likely to be exercised by hand. As with any coverage tool, the number itself is not the goal; the goal is that every risky behaviour has a test that would fail if it broke.

import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import request from "supertest";
import app from "../app.js";

test("POST /api/tutor rejects an empty question", async () => {
  const res = await request(app)
    .post("/api/tutor")
    .send({ question: "" });
  assert.equal(res.status, 400);
});

test("POST /api/tutor answers a valid question", async () => {
  const res = await request(app)
    .post("/api/tutor")
    .send({ question: "What is a closure?" });
  assert.equal(res.status, 200);
  assert.ok(res.body.reply.length > 0);
});
lessons.task: Take a small Express app, refactor it so the app is exported separately from the listen call, and write Supertest tests for one route: the success case, the empty-input 400 case, and one mocked upstream-failure case. Run them with node --test, then run with coverage and identify one untested branch worth covering.
checks: Why must the app be exported separately from listen for Supertest?
Supertest imports the app and drives it in-process without binding a port. If importing the file also starts a server, tests collide on ports and cannot run in parallel.
What does node:test give you that needs no installation?
A built-in runner with test(), describe() and mocking, discovered by node --test — part of the runtime since Node 18, so CI needs no extra dependencies.
Why mock the Gemini call in route tests?
The real call is slow, costs quota and returns varying text, making tests flaky. A stub returns a fixed reply so the test checks your route's behaviour deterministically.
How should a coverage report be read?
As a map of blind spots — untested error branches and edge cases — not as a score to maximise. The goal is tests that fail when risky behaviour breaks.
interview: How do you test an Express API without starting a server?
Export the app separately from listen, then use Supertest to send in-process requests and assert on status and body. No ports, no network, parallel-safe.
node:test versus Jest or Vitest — how do you choose?
node:test is zero-dependency and part of the runtime, ideal for backend services. Jest and Vitest add richer matchers, snapshots and frontend tooling, worth it when the project needs them.
cards: node:test
Node's built-in test runner (since Node 18): test(), describe() and mocking with no dependencies, run via node --test.
Supertest
A library that drives an Express app in-process with fake HTTP requests, asserting on status and body without a real server.
App/listen split
Exporting the Express app separately from the listen call so tests can import it without binding a port.
Stub
A fake implementation of an external dependency returning fixed results, used to keep tests deterministic.
mock.fn()
node:test's built-in mock function for replacing dependencies and asserting how they were called.
Coverage report
A listing of which lines and branches tests executed — used to find untested risky code, not as a target.

lessons.t: AI Agents & Tool Use — Beyond Single Prompts
lessons.sub: From answering to doing
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain the agent loop of plan, act and observe, define tool schemas an AI model can call, apply guardrails to agent behaviour, and design for multi-step reliability.
lessons.body:
1. From single prompt to agent loop

A single prompt is one round trip: question in, answer out. An agent is a loop: the model plans a next step, acts by calling a tool, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met or a limit stops it. That loop is what lets a model do multi-step work — search, read, compute, write — instead of only describing it. Skillzify's AI modes are single-shot by design: one question, one Gemini call, one reply. An agent version of its tutor could look up the learner's progress, fetch the relevant lesson, run their code, and then answer with all of that in hand.

2. Tools: giving the model hands

A tool is a function the model may request, described by a schema: a name, a plain-language description of when to use it, and typed parameters. The model never executes anything itself — it emits a structured request, your code validates and runs the function, and the result goes back into the conversation as an observation. Good tool design is narrow and boring: one clear job per tool, strict parameter types, and errors returned as readable text the model can react to, not stack traces.

3. Guardrails: the loop needs a fence

An agent that can act can also act wrongly, repeatedly. Guardrails bound the damage: a maximum number of steps and tokens per run, an allowlist of tools per task, human approval before irreversible actions like sending messages or spending money, and validation of every tool argument server-side — the model's output is untrusted input, exactly like a form submission. Sandboxing matters too: code execution happens in an isolated environment with no access to secrets, the same discipline Skillzify applies to running learner code.

4. Multi-step reliability: errors compound

Each step in a loop can fail, and failures compound: a 95 percent reliable step repeated 20 times succeeds only about a third of the time. Reliable agents are designed for this — small verifiable steps, checkpoints where state is saved, retries with the error fed back to the model, and a final verification step that checks the goal was actually met. Keep the loop observable: log every plan, tool call and observation, because when an agent goes wrong, the trace is the only way to see where. The honest summary: agents trade the predictability of one prompt for capability across many steps, and the engineering is all in the guardrails.

const tools = [{
  name: "get_progress",
  description: "Get a learner's XP and completed lessons by user id.",
  parameters: {
    type: "object",
    properties: { userId: { type: "string" } },
    required: ["userId"]
  }
}];

async function runAgent(goal, maxSteps = 8) {
  const history = [{ role: "user", content: goal }];
  for (let step = 0; step < maxSteps; step++) {
    const reply = await callModel(history, tools);
    if (!reply.toolCall) return reply.text;
    const result = await executeTool(reply.toolCall);
    history.push({ role: "tool", content: String(result) });
  }
  return "Stopped: step limit reached.";
}
lessons.task: Design an agent version of one Skillzify AI mode on paper: list the tools it would need with their parameter schemas, draw the plan-act-observe loop for a sample request, and write down three guardrails — a step limit, one action needing human approval, and one argument your server must validate. Then trace what happens when the second tool call fails.
checks: What are the three phases of the agent loop?
Plan: the model decides the next step. Act: it requests a tool call, which your code executes. Observe: the result returns to the model, which plans again until the goal is met or a limit stops it.
Who actually executes a tool the model requests?
Your code does. The model only emits a structured request; your server validates the arguments, runs the function, and returns the result as an observation.
Why does reliability drop so fast in long agent loops?
Step failures compound multiplicatively: even at 95 percent per step, a 20-step run succeeds only about a third of the time. Small verifiable steps and retries are the countermeasure.
Name three guardrails every production agent needs.
A step and token budget per run, an allowlist of tools per task, and human approval before irreversible actions — plus server-side validation of every tool argument.
interview: Explain the difference between a chatbot and an agent.
A chatbot answers in one round trip. An agent loops — plan, call tools, observe results — to complete multi-step goals, which adds capability and demands guardrails, budgets and observability.
How do you make a multi-step agent reliable?
Keep steps small and verifiable, checkpoint state, feed errors back for retry, cap steps and tokens, verify the final goal explicitly, and log the full trace so failures are debuggable.
cards: Agent loop
The plan-act-observe cycle a model repeats — deciding a step, calling a tool, reading the result — until the goal is met or a limit stops it.
Tool schema
The name, description and typed parameters describing a function the model may request; your code executes it.
Observation
A tool's result fed back into the conversation for the model to plan its next step from.
Guardrail
A bound on agent behaviour: step and token budgets, tool allowlists, approval gates and argument validation.
Step limit
A hard cap on loop iterations per run, preventing runaway agents from looping or spending forever.
Trace
The logged record of every plan, tool call and observation in a run — the primary debugging tool for agents.

lessons.t: Monaco Editor — The VS Code Engine in the Browser
lessons.sub: A full IDE, embedded in a web page
lessons.goal: By the end you can compare Monaco with CodeMirror, explain how language services and web workers power its intelligence, configure themes, and judge the trade-offs for an embedded code editor.
lessons.body:
1. Monaco versus CodeMirror: IDE versus component

Monaco is the editor extracted from VS Code itself: the same text model, the same IntelliSense popups, the same minimap and command palette, running in a browser tab. CodeMirror is a lighter, modular editor component designed to be embedded and extended piece by piece. The trade-off is weight versus power: Monaco ships megabytes of JavaScript and feels like an IDE out of the box; CodeMirror ships a fraction of that and lets you add exactly the features you need. Skillzify's editor is CodeMirror — a deliberate choice for a learning platform where the editor must load fast on modest phones and the lessons, not the tooling, are the product.

2. Language services: where the intelligence lives

Monaco's smarts come from language services: workers that tokenise code for syntax highlighting, validate it for error squiggles, and compute completions and hover information. For TypeScript and JavaScript these services are built in and run in web workers, so typing never blocks on analysis. For other languages, including Python, you register your own providers — a completion provider, a hover provider — or connect a language server over a socket. The architecture is the lesson: the editor renders, the services think, and the two communicate by message passing.

3. Themes, models and the editor API

Monaco separates the model (the text document) from the editor (the view), so one file can appear in two editors, or many files can live in models behind one editor with tabs. Themes are JSON rule sets mapping token types to colours, and the built-in dark and light themes match VS Code exactly — which is why learners feel at home instantly. The API surface is large: commands, decorations for highlighting ranges, diff editors, and markers for errors. That depth is Monaco's real advantage over lighter editors, and also its learning curve.

4. Workers, loading cost and the honest verdict

Monaco needs its web workers configured correctly or language features silently degrade, and its bundle must be lazy-loaded so it never taxes pages that do not show an editor. Mobile behaviour needs care: touch selection and on-screen keyboards were never its home turf. The verdict for Skillzify-style products: CodeMirror wins on load time, mobile fit and embedding simplicity; Monaco wins when the editor is the product — a full IDE experience, VS Code familiarity, and built-in TypeScript intelligence. Choosing between them is choosing what your page is for.

import * as monaco from "monaco-editor";

const editor = monaco.editor.create(document.getElementById("editor"), {
  value: "print('Hello, Skillzify')",
  language: "python",
  theme: "vs-dark",
  automaticLayout: true,
  minimap: { enabled: false }
});

editor.onDidChangeModelContent(() => {
  console.log(editor.getValue());
});
lessons.task: Embed Monaco in a test page with Python syntax highlighting and the vs-dark theme, then disable the minimap and confirm the editor resizes with its container. Write a short comparison table against CodeMirror covering bundle size, mobile behaviour, built-in language intelligence and embedding effort, and state which you would pick for Skillzify and why.
checks: Where does Monaco's IntelliSense actually run?

In web workers hosting language services, separate from the rendering thread — so analysis never blocks typing. Built-in services cover TypeScript and JavaScript; other languages need custom providers.
What is the difference between a Monaco model and an editor?
The model is the text document; the editor is the view onto it. One model can show in several editors, and many models can sit behind one editor as tabs.
Why does Skillzify use CodeMirror instead of Monaco?
It is far lighter, loads fast on modest phones, embeds simply, and the lessons are the product — Monaco's IDE weight would tax every page for features learners do not need.
What silently breaks if Monaco's workers are misconfigured?
Language features degrade — highlighting, validation and completions stop working while basic editing continues, which makes the failure easy to miss.
interview: Monaco or CodeMirror for a coding-learning platform?

CodeMirror: small bundle, fast load on low-end devices, simple embedding, and only the features the lessons need. Monaco when the editor itself is the product and VS Code-grade intelligence matters more than weight.
How does Monaco keep typing smooth while analysing code?
Language services run in web workers off the main thread; the editor sends model changes by message and renders results when they return, so keystrokes are never blocked.
cards: Monaco
The VS Code editor engine running in the browser: full IDE features, themes and IntelliSense, at the cost of a large bundle.
Language service
A worker-hosted analyser providing highlighting, validation, completions and hover info for a language.
Web worker
A background thread running JavaScript off the main thread; Monaco runs its language services there.
Editor model
Monaco's text document object, separate from the editor view — one model, many views, or many models behind tabs.
Theme
A JSON rule set mapping token types to colours; Monaco's built-ins match VS Code's dark and light themes.
CodeMirror
A lightweight, modular embeddable editor — the choice when load time and simplicity beat IDE depth.

lessons.t: Room Deep — Migrations, Relations & Offline-First Android
lessons.sub: Local data that survives upgrades and no signal
lessons.goal: By the end you can model related tables with @Relation, write a Room migration that preserves user data, observe queries as Flow, and design an offline-first sync pattern.
lessons.body:
1. Relations: modelling joined data without SQL strings

Room entities are tables; relations connect them. A learner has many progress rows, a lesson has many exercises — and @Relation lets Room fetch a parent with its children in one query, generating the join for you. You declare a data class pairing the parent entity with a list of children, annotate it with @Embedded and @Relation, and mark the DAO method @Transaction so both queries run atomically. Foreign keys with cascade deletes keep the data honest: delete a lesson and its progress rows go with it, enforced by the database rather than by hopeful code.

2. Migrations: upgrading without wiping the user

When your schema changes between app versions — a new column, a new table — Room refuses to open the old database unless you provide a migration: a Migration(1, 2) object whose migrate function runs the SQL that transforms version 1 into version 2, such as ALTER TABLE lessons ADD COLUMN difficulty TEXT. The alternative, destructive fallback, deletes the user's data on upgrade — acceptable in a prototype, unforgivable in production. Every schema change gets a migration, and every migration gets a test that opens a version-1 database and verifies the data survives. Skillzify's Android app stores lessons and progress locally, so its migrations are what stand between an update and a learner losing their streak.

3. Flow from Room: the UI that updates itself

A DAO method returning Flow<List<Lesson>> re-emits automatically whenever the underlying table changes. The UI collects the flow and re-renders; no manual refresh, no polling, no stale screens. Combined with a ViewModel exposing that flow as state, the data layer becomes reactive end to end: write progress once, and every screen observing it updates. This is the Android counterpart of the web's re-render problem — solved by the database pushing changes instead of the UI pulling them.

4. Offline-first: local truth, synced when possible

Offline-first design treats the local database as the single source of truth: the UI always reads from Room, writes go to Room immediately, and a sync layer reconciles with the server when connectivity returns. The pattern needs three decisions: how changes are queued (an outbox table of pending operations), how conflicts resolve (last-write-wins, or server-wins for shared data), and how deletions propagate (tombstones, not hard deletes, so other devices learn). For a learning app used on buses and in dead zones, offline-first is not an optimisation — it is the difference between an app that works and one that spins.

val MIGRATION_1_2 = object : Migration(1, 2) {
    override fun migrate(db: SupportSQLiteDatabase) {
        db.execSQL(
            "ALTER TABLE lessons ADD COLUMN difficulty TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'easy'"
        )
    }
}

@Dao
interface LessonDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM lessons ORDER BY id")
    fun observeLessons(): Flow<List<Lesson>>

    @Transaction
    @Query("SELECT * FROM lessons WHERE id = :id")
    suspend fun lessonWithProgress(id: String): LessonWithProgress?
}
lessons.task: In an Android project, add a difficulty column to an existing lessons table: write MIGRATION_1_2 with the ALTER TABLE statement, register it in the database builder, and write a migration test that creates a version-1 database with a row, migrates it, and asserts the row survives with the default difficulty. Then change one DAO query to return Flow and observe it updating when a row is inserted.
checks: What does @Relation do, and why does its DAO method need @Transaction?
@Relation fetches a parent entity together with its children, generating the join. @Transaction ensures the parent and child queries run atomically, so the pair is consistent.
What happens if you ship a schema change without a migration?
Room throws an IllegalStateException when opening the database — or, with destructive fallback, silently deletes all user data. Both are production failures.
How does returning Flow from a DAO change the UI's job?
Room re-emits the query result whenever the table changes, so the UI just collects and renders. No manual refresh or polling is needed.
What is an outbox table in offline-first sync?
A local table recording pending write operations made offline, which the sync layer drains to the server when connectivity returns.
interview: Explain offline-first architecture in one minute.

The local database is the single source of truth: UI reads and writes locally, always works offline, and a sync layer reconciles with the server later using an outbox queue and a stated conflict policy.
How do you test a Room migration?
Create a database at the old version with representative rows, run the migration, then open it at the new version and assert the schema matches and the data survived intact.
cards: @Relation
A Room annotation fetching a parent entity with its children in one generated join query.
Migration
A Migration(from, to) object with the SQL transforming one schema version into the next, preserving user data across upgrades.
Destructive fallback
Room's option to delete and recreate the database on schema mismatch — fine for prototypes, data loss in production.
Flow from Room
A DAO returning Flow re-emits results automatically when the table changes, making the UI reactive.
Offline-first
Architecture where the local database is the source of truth and the server is reconciled later, so the app works without connectivity.
Outbox pattern
Queueing offline writes in a local table for later sync, with tombstones propagating deletions.
